meta.title: Who really said "I don't believe in ghosts, but I've been running from them all my life"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No evidence Poe said it. The line turned up on CNN in 2006 and rewords an old ghost quip credited to Charles A. Dana and Madame de Staël.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I don't believe in ghosts, but I've been running from them all my life'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Poe. A 2006 CNN interviewee credited him with the line. It rewords an older quip credited to Charles A. Dana and Madame de Staël.

answer.label: Not Edgar Allan Poe — a reworded ghost quip
answer.authorDates: 1766–1817 · credited with the quip’s French original, not this English wording
answer.sourceLine: Poe never wrote this. The exact wording is spoken in a CNN American Morning segment of 31 October 2006 ↗ by an unidentified interviewee who says “There’s that quote from Edgar Allan Poe.” Quote Investigator ↗ traces the quip family back to Madame de Staël’s “Je n’y crois pas, mais je les crains,” which Sir Henry Holland recorded in 1872.

source.heading: Where this exact wording turns up

docMeta.dd: Halloween report by Sumi Das from Eastern State Penitentiary, Philadelphia

source.excerpt: There’s that quote from Edgar Allan Poe where he says, I don’t believe in ghosts, but I’ve been running from them all my life.
trail: 1872 — In Recollections of Past Life ↗, Sir Henry Holland records Madame de Staël saying of les revenans: “Je n’y crois pas, mais je les crains.”
1919 — In the Chicago Daily Tribune, Bert Leston Taylor credits Charles A. Dana with “I don’t believe in ghosts,” said he, “but I’ve been afraid of them all my life” (Quote Investigator ↗).
2006 — On CNN’s American Morning ↗, an unidentified interviewee says the “running from them” version and attributes it to Poe.
2008–2014 — A “chasing me my whole life” variant credited to Poe spreads online. The Poe Museum ↗ includes it in its list of quotes falsely attributed to Poe.
source.excerptNote: In the broadcast, an interviewee offers the line as something Poe said. No work by Poe contains it. The closest older English wording is the line a 1919 newspaper column credited to Charles A. Dana: “I don’t believe in ghosts,” said he, “but I’ve been afraid of them all my life.” The 2006 version has “running from” where Dana’s has “afraid of.”
source.rightsNote: No status is asserted. This English wording is an anonymous spoken paraphrase: it comes from an unidentified interviewee in a 2006 CNN broadcast, with no identifiable author or published work. Holland’s 1872 Recollections of Past Life is public domain, but it contains only the French remark, not this line.

author.name: Germaine de Staël
author.heading: About Germaine de Staël
author.metaLine: 1766–1817 · Genevan-French novelist, salon host & political theorist
author.bio: Anne Louise Germaine de Staël-Holstein, known as Madame de Staël, led salons in Paris and Geneva and wrote Corinne ou l’Italie and De l’Allemagne. Her opposition to Napoleon led to her exile from Paris. In his 1872 memoir, Sir Henry Holland recalled her saying of ghosts, “Je n’y crois pas, mais je les crains” (I don’t believe in them, but I fear them). Quote Investigator says that evidence is weakened by its late appearance.

misattribution.heading: Why Poe gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This belongs to a family of jokes about being afraid of something you say you don’t believe in. It has been credited to several people, and Poe’s name was attached only recently.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ found “no substantive evidence” that Poe used any of these quips. It says the Poe attributions “appeared long after the death of the well-known writer.” The Wikiquote page for Poe ↗ does not list the line.

In 1919, Bert Leston Taylor’s Chicago Daily Tribune column credited the newspaper editor with “I’ve been afraid of them all my life.” Quote Investigator ↗ says this remark “probably was derived directly or indirectly from the 1872 statement.”

Holland’s Recollections of Past Life ↗ (1872) records her as saying “Je n’y crois pas, mais je les crains.” Quote Investigator credits her but adds that the evidence is weakened by its late appearance.

misattribution.truthLine: Poe didn’t say it. The “running from them” wording comes from an unidentified interviewee on CNN in 2006 ↗. It rewords an older quip credited to Charles A. Dana and, before him, Madame de Staël (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: A joke that keeps changing hands
lead: The joke works the same way in every version: the speaker denies that ghosts exist and then admits to being scared of them. Quote Investigator ↗ found it in French in 1872. It then appeared in English with an unnamed “famous woman,” a Central Park policeman and Charles A. Dana, and Poe’s name was added in the 2000s.

Poe’s name suits a ghost joke, and that is probably why it stuck. Here the credit came in a Halloween TV segment about a haunted prison. An interviewee there offered the line as “that quote from Edgar Allan Poe.”

sourcesVerified.claim: QI found no substantive evidence that Poe used these quips; it says Poe ascriptions appeared long after his death; it lists the 1919 Chicago Daily Tribune Dana version ('I've been afraid of them all my life'), the 2006 CNN American Morning 'running from them' wording credited to Poe by an unidentified man, the 2008 'chasing me' tweet, and de Staël via Holland 1872 with evidence weakened by late appearance; the Dana remark probably derived from the 1872 statement

The CNN American Morning transcript of 31 Oct 2006 (Sumi Das segment, Eastern State Penitentiary) has an UNIDENTIFIED MALE saying: 'There's that quote from Edgar Allan Poe where he says, I don't believe in ghosts, but I've been running from them all my life.'
Holland's Recollections of Past Life (New York: Appleton, 1872) records Madame de Staël, speaking of les revenans: 'Je n'y crois pas, mais je les crains.'
The Poe Museum blog (Chris Semtner, 2014) lists 'I don't believe in ghosts but they have been chasing me my whole life' among quotes falsely attributed to Poe
Wikiquote's Edgar Allan Poe page does not include this ghost line in any section
Germaine de Staël: 22 April 1766 – 14 July 1817; Genevan-French novelist, salon host, political theorist; wrote Corinne and De l'Allemagne; exiled from Paris for opposing Napoleon
